correctness.rationale: For all r>=1 the established generating equation gives F(x)=(1−x)C(2x(1−x)^2), coefficient term 2^j C_j x^j(1−x)^{2j+1}. Kummer/Legendre gives v2(C_j)=s2(j+1)−1. Mod 2^r surviving polynomial terms are exactly k=j+1 with k+s2(k)<=r+1. The highest surviving summand has unique top degree 3K(r)−2 and top coefficient nonzero modulo 2^r (lower j have smaller degrees), so all a_n with n>=3K(r)−1 vanish mod 2^r, the preceding index does not: exact conductor L=3K−1. Sharp 3r−1 iff r is a power of 2. Explicit coefficients mod 32 for n=0..10 plus eventual zero after 10, together with exact small a_0..a_4, prove Rowland–Yassawi four forbidden classes for all r>=6. Independent calculations reconstructed coefficients by quadratic recursion and Catalan expansion and checked r<=16, forbidden precision r<=12; finite checks support but do not replace the formal proof.

originality.rationale: The enumeration (Le 2005), Catalan substitution (Barry 2008/OEIS), and automata (Rowland–Yassawi 2015) are earlier. No inspected later result already answers it. The derivation is elementary, but the explicit uniform conductor and open-question resolution, not the technique, are assessed as original best-of-knowledge.

value.rationale: Computing the exact last nondivisible coefficient at every 2-adic precision is an intrinsically useful arithmetic property of a classical pattern-avoidance sequence, and resolves a concrete previously posed four-residue open question. The sharp digit-sum conductor is nontrivial despite relying on a known Catalan transform; it can be used for precise congruence windows, beyond a textbook substitution.
